Hunger has a price tag Modern hunger is usually less dra- matic than a famine, which is partly why it is so easy to ignore. It looks like a market stall full of vegetables that a family cannot afford, or a bag of rice that costs a week's wages. The UN estimates that around 2.6 bil- lion people cannot afford a healthy diet. In many low-income countries, the cost of eating well exceeds what a day's work brings in. Hunger there is not a shortage of food. It is a shortage of money, arriv- ing in the shape of an empty pot. There is a bitter irony in who goes hungry. A large share of the world's un- dernourished people live in rural areas and many are farmers themselves. Smallholders often sell their harvest im- mediately after it comes in, when prices are lowest, because they need cash for debts and school fees. Months later, when their stores are gone, they buy food back at higher prices. The people who grow the food are sometimes the first to run out of it. Then come the shocks. A drought, a currency collapse or a war can turn a precarious household into a hungry one within weeks. Conflict is now among the strongest drivers of acute hunger, as fighting destroys fields, closes roads and cuts off aid. The grain may exist, sitting in a warehouse a few hours away. When something is always available, we stop attending to it. People who lived through rationing often scrape every plate and keep every crust, not from vir- tue but from memory. Abundance dulls that memory. Cheap, constant food teaches us to treat it as scenery. An honest account has to admit a limit here. A forgotten sandwich in one country does not travel to a hungry child in another. Surplus is perishable and ex- pensive to move. Cutting waste in rich countries will not directly feed anyone abroad. But it eases pressure on land, water, energy and prices and it shapes what we believe food is worth. That be- lief matters more than it seems.
What hunger does to a mind In 1944, researchers at the University of Minnesota recruited 36 healthy young men who had refused to fight on grounds of conscience. For six months, they were fed about half their usual ra- tions. The men grew gaunt, but the more startling changes were in their minds. They collected cookbooks and pored over recipes. They dreamed about meals. Some lost interest in friends, hu- mour and love, the ordinary furniture of a life. Food became the only subject left. In the city they gained something precious, which was anonymity. A young woman could es- cape a stifling family. A man could re- invent his trade. Freedom and loneliness arrived in the same suitcase and thinkers have argued about the price ever since. Hannah Arendt separated solitude, a kind of company with oneself, from loneliness, in which even that inner company falls away.
The disappearing middle ground Sociologists speak of weak ties: the newsagent, the neighbour who takes in parcels, the regular at the corner tea stall. In the 1970s Mark Granovetter showed that these light connections matter more than we assume, carrying information, opportunity and a sense of belonging. Stanley Milgram, better known for his obedience experiments, described the familiar stranger, the per- son you see on the same platform every day and never address, who still makes a place feel inhabited. Many cities are quietly thinning out this middle layer. Gated towers replace courtyards. Groceries arrive at the door, so the shopkeeper loses a customer and the customer loses a greeting. Jobs move people every few years, just as a friend- ship begins to take root. Jane Jacobs called the busy pavement a form of pub- lic safety, with many pairs of eyes keep- ing watch. Small acts, large effects The encouraging finding is that re- pair is rarely grand. In experiments by Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder, commuters asked to talk to a stranger re- ported a more pleasant journey than those who stayed silent, even though most had predicted the opposite. We consistently underestimate how wel- come we would be. Some cities are treating connection as infrastructure. Barcelona's super- blocks hand street space back to res- idents, creating squares where people can linger. Libraries, community gar- dens and shared benches give strangers a reason to stay in the same place long enough to become familiar. These are modest ideas, but familiarity is how strangers become neighbours. On a personal scale, the steps are smaller still. Learn the name of the secu- rity guard, the vendor, the person across the landing. Knock on the door of an older neighbour and leave your number. Ask the second question: after 'How are you?', try 'No, really?' None of this will feel heroic. It will feel slightly awkward, which is usually a sign that something real is happening. A lit window Walk through any city after dark and look up. Every lit window holds some- one's entire world, a kettle boiling, a phone face down, a television murmur- ing to nobody. The architecture that houses us is magnificent and strangely silent about what we owe each other. The great promise of the city was never only opportunity. It was the chance to be among others and to be known by a few of them. Density can deliver the first without any help. The second has to be built by hand, one greeting and one favour at a time.
